c1.story:
Open your phone's home screen and count the shops on it. A restaurant row, a grocery store that promises ten minutes, a beauty counter, an optician, a railway booking window, a job board, maybe a used-car lot. Indian e-commerce is not one industry. It is a mall where every tenant runs a different business model, and the listed companies in it make money in four very different ways.

The first door is the delivery marketplace: Eternal, which owns Zomato and Blinkit, Swiggy with Instamart, and Urban Company sending a plumber instead of a parcel. It takes a cut of each order and earns ad money from restaurants and brands, but it also pays a human being to carry every single order to your door. That rider is the whole drama of the business.

The second door is classifieds and listings: Naukri for jobs, IndiaMART for factory supplies, Justdial for local services, CarTrade for used cars. These platforms own no stock and deliver nothing. Recruiters and sellers pay a subscription to be seen. Once the network is the default, each extra rupee of revenue is nearly all profit.

The third door is the own-stock vertical retailer: Nykaa, Lenskart, FirstCry, Wakefit. They buy or make the product and keep the full retail margin, which means they also carry the inventory. The website is a shopfront; the real business is a brand and a category, increasingly with physical stores beside the app.

The fourth door is the toll booth: IRCTC, Ixigo, Meesho, Blackbuck. A tiny fee on an enormous number of tickets, orders or truck trips.

The same headline, orders up a lot, means four different things behind four doors.

For a delivery name it may mean losses are about to shrink, or that discounts are buying growth. For a classifieds name it means a margin already high gets higher. For a vertical retailer the question is store economics. For a toll booth the only question that really matters is whether anyone can touch the toll.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, and give the bar the most attention.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how money comes in: a cut of every order minus the rider and the dark store; a subscription or listing fee with no stock and no delivery; the full retail margin on stock the company owns; or a tiny fee per ticket, order or truck trip.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Several of them listed only in 2024 or 2025, which matters later when we get to the cycle.
  • The profit bar shows how much of each rupee the company keeps. Classifieds sit at high: no rider, no warehouse. Vertical retailers and toll booths sit at medium. Delivery marketplaces sit at low, because the last mile and the rival's discounts take most of the order value.
  • The bet line names what you are really wagering on: order frequency outrunning delivery cost; a network already being the default; a brand and a category; volume with nobody changing the toll.

Then read the analogy and the so-what below. The so-what gives you four different yardsticks: how fast losses shrink, how high margins already are, how stores perform, and how safe the toll is. The trap is to compare a delivery name's margin with a classifieds name's margin; they are not the same species.

c2.story:
Every online order, whether it is a biryani, a lipstick or a train ticket, travels through the same five stations. Where the listed companies stand in that chain explains most of their economics.

The first station is traffic. Cheap mobile data after Jio arrived in 2016, cheap smartphones and UPI payments brought hundreds of millions of Indians online. Then the platforms rent their attention back from Google, Meta and the cricket broadcasters through ads. Nobody listed in this sector owns this station; they pay a toll to it.

The second is supply: the restaurants, kiranas, brands, factories, recruiters and car dealers with something to sell. Millions of small sellers, mostly unorganised. IndiaMART and Justdial earn their living by organising them.

The third is the platform itself, the app that matches buyer and seller, takes the payment and keeps a cut. This is where Eternal, Swiggy, Meesho, Nykaa, Naukri, Lenskart and IRCTC stand. It is the only station Indian listed companies clearly own.

The fourth is fulfilment: dark stores, warehouses, gig riders and trucks moving the parcel in ten minutes or two days. Here stand the two giants that are not listed in India, Amazon and Flipkart, with networks built on foreign balance sheets, alongside Delhivery and Blackbuck's truckers.

The fifth is the customer, overwhelmingly an urban household in the big metros, plus small businesses, job seekers and travellers.

The listed names own the matchmaking. The biggest rivals own the trucks.

That geography matters more than it looks. Quick commerce makes money only where a dark store sits within a few kilometres of dense, well-off flats. That is why the top eight cities carry the economics, and why the smaller-town story is real for ticketing and social commerce but thin for ten-minute grocery. And because Amazon and Flipkart sit at the fulfilment station with patient foreign capital, every listed name's margin depends partly on how hard those two choose to fight in a given quarter.
c2.read:
Two layers: the five stations across the top, and the band row underneath that says who holds each.

The five boxes run from traffic on the left to the customer on the right. Under each you get what happens there and who stands there. Read the who lines: telcos, Google, Meta and NPCI's UPI on the left; millions of small sellers next; the listed platforms in the middle; Amazon, Flipkart, Delhivery and gig riders at fulfilment; households on the right.

The band row compresses that into one line. The first two cells, telcos and tech giants then small sellers, are plain. The coloured India listed cell sits only under the platform station. The fulfilment cell is marked Amazon and Flipkart and coloured as the rival. The last cell is urban households.

So the visual story is simple. Indian listed e-commerce is a one-station business. It rents traffic from Google and Meta on the left. On its right, the fulfilment station is where its biggest competitors are strongest, and where delivery names like Eternal and Swiggy have to build their own dark stores and rider fleets to compete.

Use it like this: when news hits any station, trace it along the row. A rise in Google ad prices is a cost shock at station one. A rider strike or a fuel price hike is a cost shock at station four. Amazon announcing a ten-minute service is a competitive shock at station four aimed straight at the delivery door.

c3.story:
Who actually pays these companies? The answer is less obvious than it looks, because the person tapping the app is often not the main customer.

Take a food delivery order. You pay for the biryani and a delivery fee, and since 2023 a small platform fee on top. But the restaurant pays too: a commission on the order, and increasingly money for ads that push it up your feed. On a quick-commerce app, the shampoo brand pays for the banner and the prime slot on the virtual shelf. Advertising is how these platforms raise their cut without raising your bill.

Then look at the classifieds door. Naukri's customer is not the job seeker, who uses it free. It is the recruiter, paying for postings and database access. That makes Naukri's revenue a direct read on white-collar hiring, which in India means largely IT services. When TCS and Infosys freeze hiring, Naukri's billings feel it within a quarter or two. IndiaMART's customer is the small factory paying for leads, which moves with small-business confidence and GST compliance. CarTrade's customer is the dealer, paying to sell used cars, which moves with used-car prices and finance rates.

Toll booths have their own customers. Travellers pay IRCTC a convenience fee per ticket, so rail capacity and holidays decide its volume. Truck owners pay Blackbuck for fuel cards, tolls and loads.

What ties nearly all of them together is that the buyer is urban and salaried. A software engineer in Bengaluru orders dinner, buys skincare, books a train home for Diwali and, eventually, updates a resume.

An IT hiring freeze is an e-commerce earnings warning, delivered a quarter early.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read each in three lines: who pays, what they pay for, and what moves them.

  • The name tells you the payer: urban households, restaurants and cloud kitchens, brands and FMCG makers, small sellers and factories, recruiters, travellers, car buyers and dealers, truck owners.
  • The middle line is what they buy. Notice how many tiles buy attention rather than goods: ad slots, listings, leads, job postings. That is the take-rate engine.
  • The last line is the watch list outside the sector: urban incomes and IT hiring, food inflation, marketing budgets, small-business confidence, rail capacity and airfares, used-car prices, freight demand and diesel.

Now map each tile to a door. Households, restaurants and brands feed the delivery marketplaces and vertical retailers. Recruiters, small sellers and car dealers feed the classifieds door. Travellers and truck owners feed the toll booths.

The pattern to notice is concentration of driver. Several tiles, households, recruiters and to a degree brands, all move with the same thing: the health of urban salaried India. A sector that looks diversified across food, jobs, beauty and travel is, underneath, one large bet on that customer. The tiles that break the pattern, truck owners and small factories, are the ones that move with the real economy rather than with the office.

c4.story:
Follow a hundred rupees of revenue through two very different platforms and you understand why the market treats them like different species.

Start with a delivery marketplace. Roughly half of the hundred goes straight out as delivery cost: the rider, packaging and the dark store that holds the groceries. Another big chunk, almost as large, goes to marketing, technology and people. Depreciation on dark stores and warehouses takes a little more. What is left is a few rupees. That is a profitable delivery platform; for years, the left-over bar was negative.

Now a classifieds site like Naukri or IndiaMART. Its input cost is almost nothing, because it delivers nothing. It spends about half its revenue on sales teams, technology and marketing. And then roughly two fifths of every rupee is left over. Same app-based business, utterly different shape.

The number delivery investors obsess over is contribution margin: what is left from each order after the rider, the packaging and the discount, before head-office costs. It is the first number to turn positive in a delivery business, and the stock trades on it. Zomato's food delivery got there first; Blinkit followed later in quick commerce.

A quarter of soaring orders with soaring marketing is bought, not earned.

Two other lines deserve attention. Employee stock options are a large non-cash charge in this sector, which is why reported profit sits far below the adjusted profit managements prefer to quote. Read both. And depreciation is rising, because the model is shifting: Blinkit moving toward owning its inventory after Eternal restructured to count as Indian-owned under the FDI rules, and vertical retailers opening stores. Owning things puts them on the balance sheet.

Interest, meanwhile, is not a cost here. Almost every listed name sits on IPO cash, so interest shows up as income.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of revenue down to what is left: delivery marketplaces on one side, classifieds and listings on the other. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is goods or delivery cost. For delivery marketplaces it takes roughly half. For classifieds it is a sliver, barely visible.
  • The opex bar is marketing, tech and people. It is large on both charts, a little over half for classifieds and somewhat under half for delivery.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small on both.
  • The last bar is what is left. This is the picture to remember: a few rupees for delivery against roughly two fifths for classifieds.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover for amounts.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Gross order value with take rate, contribution margin, marketing and discounts, and employee stock options all get a yes. Working capital, depreciation and capex are marked sometimes: marketplaces collect cash before they pay sellers, while own-stock retailers carry months of inventory. Interest gets a no, since these companies mostly hold net cash.

Then use the so-what as a three-way test each quarter. Contribution margin up with marketing flat is real operating leverage. Margin up with marketing down is harvesting. Margin flat with marketing up is a price war.

c5.story:
Most industries follow the economy. Indian e-commerce follows something else: the price of global money.

When money is cheap, investors fund platforms that burn cash on discounts to grab share, and the public market pays up for growth. When rates rise, the funding stops, the discounts stop and the weakest players fold or sell. The economy can be fine throughout; the cycle runs on the cost of capital.

The last cycle was textbook. Lockdowns in 2020 moved groceries, medicines and dinner onto the phone for good. Global money was nearly free. Zomato listed in July 2021 to a frenzy, Nykaa followed, and every category suddenly had a ten-minute delivery start-up. That was the peak: loss-making platforms at record valuations.

Then 2022. US rates rose fast, the funding winter set in and platform stocks fell by well over half. Zomato's stock sank far below its listing price, and it bought Blinkit, a struggling quick-commerce player, in an all-stock deal. Every platform swapped its growth slides for profitability slides.

The bottom came in 2023. Food delivery turned profitable. Platform fees appeared on your bill. Blinkit, the distressed purchase, turned into the surprise growth engine. The survivors began a long climb.

The best deal of the bust was a business nobody wanted at the time.

Then came a second listing wave: Ixigo, FirstCry, Swiggy and Blackbuck in 2024; Urban Company, Lenskart, Meesho and Wakefit in 2025. Quick commerce became the hottest category in Indian consumer, and the war with Zepto and Instamart peaked in losses in 2025. Today Eternal has been the year's standout large-cap as those losses narrow, and the clock sits in the boom arc: profits are real, but so are full valuations.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years are the last cycle: boom across 2020 and 2021, peak in 2021, bust in 2022, bottom in 2023. The arrow points into the boom arc, labelled second listing wave. The detail line says it plainly: profits arriving, valuations full, the quick-commerce war easing. Hover any arc to read what defined it.

The timeline runs from 2019. Notice the colours: a boom stretch for 2020 and 2021, a bust entry in 2022, a neutral bottom in 2023, a fresh boom in 2024, then a neutral 2025 when the quick-commerce war peaked and a crowd of companies listed, and the latest entry marked now.

The four hands are how you move the arrow yourself.

  • Quick-commerce contribution margin: turning positive, arrow up. A fresh dip would mean a new entrant is spending.
  • Marketing cost to revenue: falling, arrow up. Growth is becoming organic.
  • US ten-year yield: easing, arrow up. Lower yields support long-duration growth stocks, but also reopen funding for rivals.
  • Dark-store additions: slowing, mixed. Slowing means harvesting; a renewed surge means another round of burn.

Three hands point up and one is mixed. That fits a boom with real economics underneath, where the risk is less the business and more the price.

c6.story:
Here is a slightly uncomfortable fact for anyone who owns Indian platform stocks: the single most important number for their valuation is set in Washington, not Delhi.

The first three-dot dial is the US ten-year Treasury yield. Platform profits are expected to arrive years from now, and the further away a profit is, the more its present value depends on the discount rate. When the US yield rises, long-duration growth stocks everywhere fall, Indian platforms included. The yield also controls the global funding tap: when it is low, venture money flows to rivals, and rivals spend it on discounts. That is why this dial carries a diamond. Lower yields lift your multiple and arm your competitors at the same time.

The second three-dot dial is urban salaried incomes and IT hiring. This one is about orders, not multiples. More software jobs mean more dinners ordered, bigger baskets and more Naukri billings. It is the closest thing this sector has to a demand dial.

The two-dot dials sharpen the picture. Fuel prices raise the cost of every delivery and squeeze contribution margin. Food inflation fattens the rupee value of a grocery basket but trims how often people order. The RBI policy rate shapes consumer credit and the domestic appetite for growth stocks. Risk appetite, which you can watch through India VIX, widens or narrows the premium on recently listed loss-makers. And two rule-shaped dials matter a lot: FDI policy, which has kept Amazon and Flipkart from owning inventory on their marketplaces and so gave Indian-owned platforms an edge, and gig-worker and GST rules, each of which adds a few rupees to every order.

The one-dot dials are slower: the rupee nudges foreign flows, and smartphone penetration keeps adding new users from smaller towns.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the business. This column tells you whether a dial moves the multiple, the order book or the cost per order. The US yield and risk appetite move the multiple; urban incomes, food inflation and the policy rate move orders and baskets; fuel and gig-worker rules move the cost per order.
  • A rise does: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it cuts both ways. The US yield and food inflation carry diamonds here.
  • Weight: one to three dots.

The last column shows today's reading where we track a matching series: the US ten-year yield, the Nifty IT index as a stand-in for IT hiring, the money-market rate, Brent crude for fuel, food CPI, India VIX and the rupee. FDI policy, gig-worker and GST rules and smartphone penetration show a dash; those you follow through the news.

Read the three-dot rows first: the US yield and urban hiring. One sets the price the market pays for these companies, the other sets how many orders they get. If both move against you in the same quarter, as they did in 2022, the stocks fall regardless of execution.

Then scan the red two-dot rows, fuel and gig-worker rules, because they hit contribution margin directly.

c7.story:
Why can't a delivery platform simply grow its way to the margins of a classifieds site? Because of the bottlenecks, and the first one rides a motorbike.

Every order is carried by a human. The cost per delivery falls only with density: more orders per rider per hour, more orders per dark store per day. Below a certain density, every extra order adds losses rather than profit. That is why quick commerce works in dense metro neighbourhoods and struggles almost everywhere else. It is structural; no app update changes it.

The second structural bottleneck is the competition's balance sheet. Amazon and Flipkart, the latter owned by Walmart, are not listed in India and are funded by foreign parents who can lose money here for a decade. Price discipline in Indian e-commerce is borrowed from them, not owned by the listed companies.

Then the cyclical one: funding-driven competition. Whenever global money is cheap, a new entrant arrives with discounts. Zepto did it in quick commerce. Rapido is now doing it in food delivery. Each time, incumbents must choose between matching the discounts and losing share.

The recurring bottlenecks are mostly rules and real estate. The FDI line between marketplace and inventory gets redrawn every few years. Gig-worker welfare laws, starting in Rajasthan in 2023 and then Karnataka, plus the labour codes and GST on delivery fees, each add a few rupees per order, which can be the entire contribution margin. The right dark-store location near rich flats is scarce, and rents climb with every competitor's expansion. And trader associations lobby against deep discounting, with a government that listens before elections.

In delivery, density is the moat and the rider is the meter.

The slow one is stock-option dilution: large annual grants quietly transfer a slice of the company from shareholders to employees, year after year.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. Use the label to decide where each risk belongs.

  • Structural: last-mile cost and Amazon and Flipkart's balance sheets. These cap delivery margins permanently, so they belong in your valuation. Notice both hit the delivery door far harder than classifieds, which has no rider and no foreign giant in most of its categories.
  • Cyclical: funding-driven competition. This one tracks the US yield dial from the wiring diagram. When money gets cheap, expect a new discounter within a year.
  • Recurring: foreign-ownership policy, gig-worker regulation, dark-store real estate and kirana pushback. These are the headlines that hit a quarter. Each one shaves rupees off the cost per order or changes who may own stock.
  • Slow: stock-option dilution, a quiet annual leak rather than an event.

Read the so-what under the table as a reading order. The first two rows set the ceiling for delivery margins. The funding row tells you when the next price war starts, which is why the so-what says to watch rivals' fund-raises as closely as results.

One practical test: for each company you own, count how many of these rows apply. A classifieds name may face only the stock-option row. A quick-commerce name faces nearly all of them.

c8.story:
Indian e-commerce has been shaped by its rulebook more than almost any other consumer sector, and one rule built the whole competitive landscape.

That rule is the FDI policy on e-commerce. Foreign-owned platforms may run a marketplace, but may not own the inventory they sell. A tightened press note issued in 2018, which bit from February 2019, also barred them from favouring sellers they had stakes in. Amazon and Flipkart had to restructure around it. Indian-owned platforms face no such limit, which is precisely why Eternal capped its foreign shareholding in 2025 so it would count as Indian-owned and controlled, letting Blinkit own its own stock. One policy, and a large company rearranged its shareholder register.

Then the rules that nibble at the margin. Since January 2022, food delivery platforms have collected and paid the GST on restaurant food themselves. From the 2025 GST changes, delivery fees through platforms carry GST too, paid either from the contribution margin or by the customer. State gig-worker laws and the labour codes ask platforms to fund rider welfare through a levy per transaction. FSSAI is moving to make online food players directly accountable for what restaurants and dark stores sell.

Consumer rules limit the tricks that lift conversion: the CCPA's 2023 guidelines against dark patterns, rules against fake reviews. The Competition Commission has investigated Amazon and Flipkart over preferred sellers and exclusive launches.

And then the toll booth's whole profit. IRCTC's convenience fee was waived after demonetisation in 2016 and restored in 2019. In October 2021, the railway ministry ordered IRCTC to share half of it; the stock crashed, and the order was withdrawn the next morning.

When your profit is a fee, the person who can waive it is your biggest risk factor.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and its status.

The status column sets your priorities.

  • Always: the DPIIT's FDI policy on e-commerce and the railway ministry's mandate for IRCTC. These are foundations, not news, but when either changes, a business model changes with it. The FDI row is the one that gave Indian-owned platforms their edge.
  • Live: the consumer affairs department and CCPA, the Competition Commission and ONDC. These shape behaviour today: dark-pattern bans, antitrust probes, and an open network that could pressure take rates if it ever scales.
  • New: the GST Council and CBIC row, with GST now charged on delivery services through platforms. This one lands directly on cost per order.
  • Coming: labour codes and state gig-worker laws, FSSAI accountability for online food, and a proposed ex-ante digital competition law on the EU model. These are the rules to prepare for. Two of the three raise cost per order; the third could restrict self-preferencing by the biggest players.

Notice which door each row hits. Most land on the delivery marketplaces. The railway row is entirely about one toll booth. Classifieds barely appear, which is part of why that door keeps the most profit.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces boils down to a question every platform investor should ask: once the order comes in, who gets to keep the money?

Run a delivery marketplace through it and it struggles on almost every spoke. Rivalry is maximal: two or three platforms fight for the same flat, with the same riders and the same discounts. Buyers are fickle: most urban households keep two delivery apps and switch for a coupon. Suppliers have options: riders can switch apps mid-shift, and restaurants can delist or push their own ordering. Entrants keep coming, because a well-funded newcomer can buy share in delivery within a year. And substitutes are real: the neighbourhood kirana, the restaurant's own app, and ONDC.

Now run Naukri through the same test. Rivalry is low because a classifieds leader is usually alone in its category. Recruiters have nowhere else with the same pool of resumes, and job seekers go where the recruiters are. That is a network effect: each side attracts the other, and the leader gets stronger simply by being the leader. Building a rival classifieds network from scratch has failed repeatedly in India. LinkedIn and the big IT firms' own job portals nibble at the edges, but they nibble.

A delivery app rents its customers. A classifieds leader owns its market.

That contrast explains a paradox in how the market prices these businesses. Classifieds earn high margins at a lower multiple, because their growth is steady and their market is mature. Delivery leaders earn thin margins at a very high multiple, because investors are paying for the possibility that density and scale eventually tame the forces that squeeze them today.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the business. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: delivery marketplaces and classifieds and listings. This is one of the starkest contrasts on any industry page. Look at the overall size first: the delivery shape is far larger than the classifieds shape in every direction. The classifieds shape hugs the centre.

  • Rivalry: delivery hits the outer ring; classifieds sits near the centre. This is the widest gap on the chart.
  • Buyer: delivery reaches well out, because customers switch for a coupon. Classifieds stays modest; a recruiter cannot leave the biggest resume pool.
  • Supplier: delivery sits in the middle, riders and restaurants can walk; classifieds sits near the centre.
  • Entrants: delivery in the middle, classifieds near the centre.
  • Substitutes: the closest the two shapes come. Both face some substitution: the kirana for one, LinkedIn for the other.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a one-line reason. Vertical retailers and toll booths are not drawn, but you can place them yourself: a toll booth like IRCTC would have a tiny shape everywhere except one spoke, the regulator behind the supplier and buyer lines.

c10.story:
An e-commerce results release can run to dozens of slides of gross order value, cohorts, cities and dark-store maps. Eight numbers tell you most of what matters, and they are designed to catch the classic tricks.

Gross order value growth comes first: the total value flowing through the platform, before the platform's cut. It shows whether the network is still compounding. Then the take rate, how much of that flow the platform keeps, including ads. A rising take rate driven by ads is the healthiest kind, because the customer's bill does not change.

The heart of the matter is contribution margin per order: what is left after the rider, the packaging and the discount. This is where unit economics live or die. Then adjusted EBITDA margin, which adds head office, marketing and tech. Expanding every quarter means operating leverage is real.

Marketing as a share of revenue is the honesty check. If orders soar while marketing soars, growth was bought. Monthly transacting users and order frequency tell you about the network itself: more users ordering more often is the dream.

Then two numbers managements prefer you skip. Employee cost including stock options is the gap between the adjusted profit in the headline and the reported profit in the accounts. And net cash against quarterly burn tells you how many quarters of war a company can fund before it needs the market's help.

Adjusted EBITDA is what the company wants you to see. Stock options are what it costs you to see it.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to put to each company. Several rows exist to separate earned growth from bought growth: take rate, contribution margin, marketing share.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, as rules of thumb. Several are door-specific: gross order value growth has separate bars for quick commerce and food delivery; adjusted EBITDA has a high bar for classifieds; order frequency is a food-delivery measure.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of listed companies. Only three rows have one: sales growth, EBITDA margin and employee cost. The rest, take rate, contribution margin, marketing share, users and frequency, net cash against burn, are operating metrics found in investor presentations rather than in filings, so they show a dash.

A caution on the medians: they blend loss-making delivery names, very profitable classifieds and steady toll booths. The EBITDA median in particular can sit between doors and describe none of them well. Always compare a company with its own door's good mark first.

The best routine: each quarter, put contribution margin, marketing share and stock-option cost side by side for your names. That trio tells you whether growth is earned and whether the profit is real.

c11.story:
The earliest warnings in Indian e-commerce rarely come from the platforms themselves. They come from venture-funding headlines, IT company hiring calls, FMCG results and bond markets on the other side of the world.

Some signals arrive in the same quarter. The US ten-year yield and Nasdaq growth multiples move Indian platform stocks the same month, whether or not anything changed in Indian ordering. Rail passenger volumes and airfares move IRCTC's and Ixigo's fees as tickets are sold.

Most useful signals speak one quarter ahead. A rival's fund-raise or dark-store announcement means discounts within a quarter, and margins follow. IT services hiring and attrition commentary is next quarter's Naukri billings and the urban order budget. When FMCG companies talk about how much of their sales now go through quick commerce, they are telling you where grocery spend is moving before the platforms report. Fuel prices and rider wage disputes raise last-mile cost a quarter later. Used-car prices and auto finance rates lead CarTrade's dealer demand.

The furthest dot is policy: GST Council and labour-code announcements take a quarter or two to pass through or be absorbed.

Combine the big ones and you get the three-sign rule. The rally rests on fundamentals when contribution margins are expanding, marketing as a share of revenue is falling, and global yields are steady or lower. Right now all three are ticking, though the yield tick carries a note to watch for a reversal.

Three ticks is a boom with real profits under it. It is also the moment the market stops forgiving misses.

That is why the call favours leaders with proven unit economics and the asset-light classifieds names, and treats freshly listed loss-makers as execution bets priced for perfection.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to see its channel into earnings.

  • Same quarter, far left: the US ten-year yield with Nasdaq multiples, and rail passenger volumes with airfares. These describe what is happening now.
  • One quarter ahead: the crowded middle. Rival fund-raises and dark-store announcements, IT hiring and attrition commentary, FMCG companies' quick-commerce commentary, fuel prices and rider wage disputes, used-car prices and auto finance rates.
  • Two quarters ahead: GST Council and labour-code announcements, the earliest warning on this chart.

Use it as a reading order. Check the policy dot on the right first, then sweep the one-quarter cluster, paying most attention to rival fund-raises, because a funded competitor is the fastest way for a delivery name's margins to reverse. The left-hand dots are for confirmation.

Below the chart is the rule with three signs. All three carry ticks: contribution margins expanding as quick commerce turns positive, marketing share falling as discounts fade, and global yields easing, with a note to watch for a reversal. Three of three is the rule's strongest reading.

Then the call box: the headline, three points, and what would change the call: a sharp rise in global yields, a new well-funded quick-commerce entrant, or a rewrite of the FDI or digital-competition rules. Make those three your news alerts.
